name: Economy of Motion
description: Use purposeful grips, frames, and weight shifts in BJJ to reduce repeated effort, while keeping the movement and urgency that a changing position needs.
summary: Economy of motion means using movement to change the position, rather than repeatedly spending effort on an obstacle you have not removed.
overview: If you have bridged three times and landed in the same pin, a harder fourth attempt may not answer the problem. Look at what stayed fixed and what space the next movement needs to create.
key_takeaways: Give each grip a job. Release or replace it when it no longer controls something useful.
Connect movements: use the space a bridge creates for the next action instead of returning to the same shape.
Adjust your support as weight moves rather than holding one rigid posture through the whole exchange.
Efficient does not always mean small or slow. A large movement can be appropriate when it solves the actual problem.
Use the result to judge effort: did you improve your angle, recover a barrier, or remove a post?

bjj_applications.scenario: You keep pushing a side-control partner away with your arms.
bjj_applications.application: Inspect where your elbows and hips are. Rebuild the frames your coach has taught, then use the space they preserve to move your hips and recover a knee.
bjj_applications.outcome: The arm effort supports a specific recovery instead of an indefinite push.

bjj_applications.scenario: You grip a sleeve tightly after your partner has already changed position.
bjj_applications.application: Ask what the grip now prevents. If it no longer limits their movement or helps your attack, replace it with a grip that serves the current exchange.
bjj_applications.outcome: Your hands stop working to preserve a connection you no longer need.

bjj_applications.scenario: You circle around open guard but the opponent turns with every step.
bjj_applications.application: First control a leg or create an angle that makes their turn harder. Move when that control changes the relationship between their knees and your path.
bjj_applications.outcome: You can judge the pass by progress rather than the distance you ran.

common_mistakes.mistake: Trying to win a prize for moving the least.
common_mistakes.consequence: Stillness can let the opponent settle a grip or pin.
common_mistakes.correction: Move as much as the position requires; remove repetition that does not change it.

common_mistakes.mistake: Relaxing every muscle because frames should carry the load.
common_mistakes.consequence: A frame can collapse or drift out of place when you stop managing its alignment.
common_mistakes.correction: Use the tension needed to keep the frame useful, and adjust it as the force changes.

training_exercises.name: Find the wasted repetition
training_exercises.description: Start in a familiar pin with agreed resistance. Attempt your taught escape and reset after recovery or a stopped attempt. Have your partner identify a repeated movement that left the position unchanged; alter its setup or follow-up on the next attempt.
training_exercises.focus: Link effort to a visible change in position.

knowledge_assessment.question: When is a large movement economical?
knowledge_assessment.answer: When its size is needed to create the space, angle, or off-balance you can actually use, without unnecessary repetitions.
